CausalChain: Chronic liver inflammation -> induces DNA methylation alterations in hepatocytes -> leads to aberrant expression of regulatory genes -> alters exosomal microRNA cargo released into circulation -> modulates the tumor microenvironment by affecting immune checkpoint molecules (e.g., PD-L1) -> influences responsiveness to immunotherapy
Hypothesis: Circulating exosomal microRNA profiles, reflective of early DNA methylation changes induced by chronic hepatic inflammation, are predictive biomarkers for both early HCC development and response to immunotherapy by modulating the tumor immune microenvironment.
Abstract: Recent advances in the study of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) have underscored the limitations of traditional serum biomarkers for early detection and treatment selection. We propose that circulating exosomal microRNA signatures, which are modulated by early epigenetic alterations such as DNA methylation changes in hepatic cells subjected to chronic inflammation, may serve as dual-function biomarkers. These exosomal microRNAs could not only predict early oncogenic transformation in HCC but also modulate the tumor immune microenvironment, thereby influencing response to immunotherapy. This hypothesis integrates the complex interplay between chronic liver injury, epigenetic modifications, and exosome-mediated cell–cell communication, offering a novel, testable approach to enhance both early diagnosis and personalized therapeutic strategies in HCC.
